{"content": [{"text": "Yes—this is now a real implementation of the algorithm, not merely the occlusion foundation. The latest head adds 17 coverage-engine files, a worker, UI, and tests. Joint mode genuinely evaluates candidate pairs rather than greedily selecting the best first origin.

Revised verdict

Algorithm architecture for normal graybox sets: 8/10

Correctness of the two search modes: 7.5/10

Readiness for complex imported sets: 4/10

Overall: promising, but I would not merge it as production-ready yet.


The math/search design is mostly right. The blockers are implementation scale and one dangerous workflow decision.

What it got right

The surface sampler is deterministic and correctly samples triangles in proportion to world-space area using barycentric coordinates.

Origin evaluation includes:

actual segment occlusion,

geometric face normals,

viewing angle,

approximate projected texel density,

separate visibility and usable-coverage bitsets,

continuous quality values.


That closely follows the algorithm we designed.

The joint-pair mode is genuinely joint. It checks every legal coarse pair, ranks them by bitset union, and only then applies quality and contribution tie-breakers. It does not discard individually mediocre but complementary origins prematurely.

The shared coarse-to-fine engine is also sensibly organized:

4,096 coarse samples,

256 candidates,

retained pair seeds,

24,576 fine samples,

local offsets,

separate fixed-first and joint branches.


The tests cover deterministic sampling, double-sided occlusion, marginal second-origin ranking, non-greedy pair ranking, candidate generation, and both search modes.

Blockers

1. Imported sets can produce zero legal candidates

This is the biggest correctness issue.

For every non-floor scene object, the extractor stores the entire object’s axis-aligned bounding box as an obstacle.

Candidate clearance is then the distance from the origin point to those bounding boxes, and candidates within 0.3 meters are rejected. A point anywhere inside an AABB has a distance of zero.

Consider a typical imported model:

Imported Set
├── floor
├── walls
├── furniture
└── props

PanoRef represents that as one imported SceneObject. Its AABB may enclose the entire room. Every sensible camera origin inside the room is therefore “inside the obstacle bounds,” gets zero clearance, and is rejected.

This can affect:

a complete Maya set imported as one GLB,

a room shell and furniture combined into one mesh,

concave geometry,

L-shaped walls,

any large model whose AABB contains empty navigable space.


Fix

Use actual geometry clearance, not object AABBs:

candidate valid =
    camera sphere/capsule does not intersect nearby triangles

The coverage BVH can support this through point-to-triangle distance, sphere intersection, or a shapecast. At minimum, obstacle bounds should be per connected mesh or spatial cluster—not per imported set object.

Add a regression test with one imported object containing a room floor, walls, and empty interior.

2. The geometry representation will not scale to heavy imports

Every triangle is expanded into a JavaScript object containing:

three independent Vec3 arrays,

a normal array,

IDs,

area.


For 3 million triangles, even an ideal packed representation would require approximately:

Positions: 3,000,000 × 9 × 4 bytes = 108 MB
Normals:   3,000,000 × 3 × 4 bytes =  36 MB
                                           ──────
Minimum packed geometry data:              144 MB

The actual representation uses JavaScript objects, arrays, and 64-bit numbers, so it will be several times larger. It is then structured-cloned into the worker with postMessage, temporarily creating another enormous representation.

The BVH also recursively sorts and slices JavaScript index arrays.

Worse, every triangle intersection allocates several temporary three-element arrays. Millions of candidate/sample raycasts will create extreme garbage-collection pressure.

This will probably work on the default graybox. I would expect serious freezing, memory spikes, or crashes on the heavy imported projects that previously hit PanoRef’s multi-million-triangle limits.

Fix

Use compact typed arrays:

interface PackedCoverageGeometry {
  positions: Float32Array;
  indices: Uint32Array;
  normals?: Float32Array;
  meshRanges: Uint32Array;
  transforms: Float32Array;
}

Transfer ArrayBuffers into the worker rather than cloning nested objects.

For the BVH, either:

use three-mesh-bvh,

implement a flat typed-array BVH with in-place partitioning,

or build per-mesh BVHs from the existing indexed geometries.


Also avoid expanding indexed vertices into three world-space vertex arrays per triangle.

3. Geometry extraction still blocks the main thread

The panel synchronously calls extractCoverageScene(project) before creating/posting to the worker.

So the worker keeps the expensive optimizer off the UI thread, but not:

scene recreation,

triangle flattening,

world-transform application,

geometry disposal,

structured cloning.


On a complex model, the app may freeze before the worker even reports its first progress event.

The extraction itself needs to move into the worker, or at least become chunked and yield between meshes.

4. “Apply to selected panorama pair” is conceptually wrong

The UI allows the optimized origins to be written directly into the two existing panorama references.

The workspace handler literally changes their stored origins:

updatePanoReference(primaryPanoId, { origin: originA });
updatePanoReference(secondaryPanoId, { origin: originB });

But an existing panorama was rendered or generated from its original origin. Changing its metadata does not transform the image into a panorama captured from the new position. It merely projects the old pixels from the wrong point, ruining alignment.

Correct workflow

For fixed-first:

1. Preserve the existing panorama and its origin.


2. Move the next capture origin to B.


3. Render a new graybox panorama.


4. Inpaint/generate the new styled panorama.


5. Import it as the secondary panorama.



For joint mode:

1. Create a two-origin capture plan.


2. Move capture origin to A.


3. Capture/render A.


4. Move to B.


5. Capture/render B.


6. Associate each imported result with its actual origin.



Do not rewrite the origins of already captured panoramas.

5. The reachable upper bound is mathematically inconsistent

reachableCoverage is calculated using the coarse sample bank and all coarse candidates.

The final combined coverage is calculated using a different fine sample bank generated with seed + 1.

Those two percentages are then placed together in the same result and used to calculate reachable efficiency.

Therefore, the UI can theoretically show:

Combined coverage:        83%
Reachable upper bound:    80%
Reachable captured:      100%

The clamp hides the impossible ratio but does not repair the incompatible estimates.

There is another fixed-first issue: the reachable set is calculated before the arbitrary first origin is evaluated, so the fixed first origin is not included in the reachable upper bound at all.

Fix

Use a common validation sample bank for both:

final pair coverage,

reachable candidate union,

efficiency.


For fixed-first, include the fixed origin in the reachable union.

You can still use separate coarse and fine search banks internally, but reported metrics must be evaluated on one shared final bank.

6. Fixed-first does not enforce minimum separation

Joint mode rejects pairs below minimumOriginSeparation.

Fixed-first mode does not. rankSecondOrigins only filters by object identity, not position or distance. Since the first evaluation is a separate object, even an identical candidate position survives.

Add:

distance(first.position, candidate.position) >= minimumOriginSeparation

Otherwise an open set with little marginal difference could return a nearly duplicate second origin.

Important refinements

The “four-level refinement” is not truly iterative

For every seed, all offsets are generated around the original seed:

seed ± spacing/2
seed ± spacing/4
seed ± spacing/8
seed ± spacing/16

The system does not select the best half-step result and then center the quarter-step search around that new result.

It is still a useful multiresolution neighborhood sample, but it is not the coordinate/pattern refinement described in the plan. A true refinement loop would update the center after every level.

Local candidates can float between floors

Candidate validation only checks whether a floor exists somewhere below the candidate.

Local offsets retain the original Y coordinate.

On sloped terrain or multilevel sets, an offset can move over a lower floor while preserving the upper floor’s camera height, leaving the panorama origin floating several meters above the new floor.

For each offset:

1. find the floor under the new X/Z,


2. set Y = floorY + panoramaHeightMeters,


3. then perform clearance.



The optimizer and runtime renderer use different quality rules

The optimizer evaluates angle and texel density.

But when both panoramas are visible, the actual shader still blends them only by distance.

Thus the optimizer may prefer a source for its frontal angle, while the runtime renderer favors the closer but more grazing source. The optimized coverage result and the visible result do not fully agree.

The shader should use the same approximate quality function and preferably winner-takes-most selection rather than broad continuous averaging.

Testing assessment

The current tests are good unit tests, but the most dangerous cases are absent:

1. One large imported object containing an entire room.


2. A 100k+ triangle performance fixture.


3. reachableCoverage >= combinedCoverage invariant.


4. Fixed-first candidate separation.


5. Sloped and multilevel floors.


6. Existing panorama origins remaining immutable.


7. Candidate generation inside concave imported geometry.



There are no GitHub Actions workflow runs attached to the latest head, so the reported test suite has not been independently enforced in CI.

Bottom line

This push is much better than what I reviewed before. The two algorithms are truly implemented, and the joint search is not fake or merely greedy.

I would preserve most of the high-level design. The required changes are:

1. Replace AABB clearance with actual geometry clearance.


2. Replace object-heavy triangle/BVH data with typed arrays and transferable buffers.


3. Move extraction into the worker.


4. Remove the ability to relocate existing panorama references.


5. Recalculate reported metrics on one common sample bank.


6. Enforce separation in fixed-first mode.


7. Reproject local refinement candidates onto their floor.



After those, I’d consider the optimizer a strong, credible feature. Right now it should work nicely on ordinary PanoRef primitive sets, but the exact scenario motivating this feature—a complex imported production set—is where the current implementation is most likely to fail.", "type": "input_text"}], "id": "msg_019f7a39-d7c2-7e43-aac5-0ea88bf33f00", "internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough": {"turn_id": "019f7a39-d71c-7e21-aaa4-685650c8467a"}, "role": "user", "type": "message"}
